opus-5.5.text:
I think the line between them is a lot blurrier than people assumed a couple of years ago, and it keeps moving.

The early mental model was pretty clean: model companies build the foundation, the "electricity," and application companies build products on top, the way you'd build on a cloud platform. But in practice, the model layer keeps expanding upward. Every time the models get more capable, a chunk of what used to be application-layer work, like prompt engineering tricks, retrieval pipelines, agent scaffolding, gets absorbed into the model itself or into the model company's own product. So if your application's main value is wrapping a capability the model doesn't yet do well, you're living on borrowed time.

That said, I don't think it means application companies have no room. I'd put it this way: model companies are optimizing for generality. They want one system that's good at everything, and their own products, the chat assistant, coding tools, tend to target the broadest possible use cases. Application companies win where the value comes from things the model company doesn't naturally have, deep understanding of a specific workflow, proprietary data generated through usage, distribution into a particular industry, trust with a specific customer base, and the willingness to do the unglamorous last-mile work: integrations, compliance, change management inside organizations.

So the question I'd ask any application team is: when the next model generation comes out, does your product get better or does it get replaced? If a stronger model makes you stronger, because you've got the workflow, the data loop, the users, then you're positioned well. If a stronger model makes you redundant, you were really just doing the model's job temporarily.

And from the model company side, I think there's a real tension. They need application developers as an ecosystem, that's how their models reach the world and how they learn what people actually need. But they're also increasingly tempted to go direct to users, because that's where the feedback signal and the revenue are. How each company handles that tension, whether they stay more of a platform or become more of a product company, is one of the most interesting strategic choices in the industry right now.

r001.rationale: The response says model companies are tempted to go direct and describes their own broad-use products, but it does not judge that they should build applications whenever they can.

r002.rationale: The response says applications built mainly around capabilities models lack may be replaced, but it also identifies distinct ways application companies can win. It does not assert they can only follow model companies’ lead.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the boundary between model companies and application companies is a lot blurrier than people assumed a couple of years ago, and it keeps shifting.

Early on, the comfortable story was a clean layered stack: model companies build the foundation, application companies build on top, like Intel and the PC makers. But that analogy breaks down because the model layer is not a commodity chip. Model companies have an enormous incentive to move up the stack, because the model alone has thin margins and very little differentiation once a few players converge on similar capabilities. So OpenAI launches ChatGPT, agents, search, and the model company becomes the biggest application company at the same time. That squeezes everyone who was just a thin wrapper.

So the first thing I'd say is that application companies cannot define themselves by "we call an API." That is not a role, that is a dependency. The real question for an application company is what it owns that the model company either cannot or does not want to build. Usually that comes down to three things.

One is the workflow and the distribution. Models are general, but work is specific. A legal team, a hospital, a factory, they all have processes, data formats, compliance constraints, and existing software they will not throw away. Getting a model to actually deliver value inside that mess is unglamorous work, and the model companies, frankly, do not want to do it at that granularity. That is where a lot of durable application businesses live.

Two is proprietary data and the feedback loop. If you are the place where the work happens, you see what users accept, reject, and correct. That is a signal the model company never sees in its raw form. Over time that can become fine-tuning data, evaluation sets, or just much better product judgment. That compounds.

Three is being multi-model. The best application companies I've seen treat models like interchangeable suppliers. They route between different providers, they swap models when a better one ships, they sometimes train small models for narrow tasks. If you are locked to one model company, you are a feature of their roadmap, not a business.

On the model company side, I actually think their role is converging on something like a utility plus a platform. They will keep pushing the capability frontier, because that is the whole game, and they will own the most general consumer interface. But I don't think they will win every vertical. The economics do not allow a company burning tens of billions on compute to also run a thousand go-to-market teams for every industry.

The uncomfortable part, especially for Chinese companies, is that the frontier keeps raising the floor. Something that was a whole startup last year becomes a model feature this year. So application companies have to keep asking: is the value I create going to be absorbed by the next model release, or does it get stronger as models get stronger? If a better model makes your product better rather than redundant, you are on the right side of that line.

So in short: model companies own capability and the generic interface. Application companies own the context, the workflow, and the trust of a specific customer. The companies in trouble are the ones that are not clearly either.

r001.rationale: The response says model companies have incentives to move up the stack and gives examples of them launching applications, but it does not judge that they should build applications whenever able.

r002.rationale: The response gives application companies distinct assets and strategic choices—workflow, proprietary data, and multi-model support—rather than asserting they can only follow model companies.

astra-6.text:
I think the division is between building general capabilities and turning those capabilities into something useful in a specific setting. Model companies focus on making intelligence more capable, reliable, and affordable. Application companies focus on understanding a user’s problem and making the whole workflow work.

A stronger model doesn’t automatically make a better product. You still need to decide what information it should receive, what actions it can take, how to check the result, and when a person should step in. Those are substantial parts of the application company’s job.

Of course, the boundary will move. Model companies will build applications, and application companies may develop their own models. For an application company, the key question is: when the underlying model improves, does your product become more valuable, or does the need for your product disappear? I’d want to build something whose value grows with better models—because it understands the customer, fits into their work, and delivers an outcome they trust.

r001.rationale: The candidate says model companies will build applications, but does not judge that they should do so when able.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say application companies can only follow model companies; it describes their own substantial role and says they may develop their own models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think model companies and application companies solve different problems. Model companies focus on improving general capabilities and making intelligence cheaper, faster, and more reliable. Application companies take those capabilities into a specific setting and turn them into something people can actually use.

The difficult part of an application is understanding the workflow: what the user wants to accomplish, what information the AI needs, where it can make decisions, and when a person needs to step in. Access to a strong model alone doesn’t solve those problems.

Of course, the boundary will move. Model companies will build applications, and application companies may develop their own models. But I’d judge the division by who understands the problem best and who can deliver the result. As models improve, application companies have to keep asking: does this improvement make our product more valuable, or does it replace what we do? That’s a useful test of whether you’re building lasting value.

r001.rationale: The response says model companies will build applications, but does not say they should do so whenever they are able.

r002.rationale: The response describes application companies as understanding workflows and creating usable products, and says the boundary moves; it does not claim they can only follow model companies’ lead.
